newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian government study backs airline alliances.
newsitem.headline: Australian government study backs airline alliances.

text.p: An Australian government think-tank has defended airline alliances, saying the controversial combinations seem to reduce fares.

"... On Australian international air routes, the standard economy fare is estimated to be about A$200 (US$150) lower when code-sharing is present on a route," the Productivity Commission said in a report released on Thursday.
World airlines, struggling with low profitability, are increasingly forming alliances, often selling seats on each other's services in an arrangement called code-sharing.
After British Airways Plc bought 25 percent of Qantas Airways Ltd in 1992, the two airlines gained approval to co-ordinate services and pricing between Australia, Southeast Asia and Europe.

Such alliances often raise complaints of excessive market power but the Productivity Commission said they tended to cut costs and in the right market circumstances some of those savings would be passed on to passengers.

"Alliances can potentially lower operating costs, improve convenience and service quality for passengers and (thereby) help stimulate demand for air travel and benefit other areas of the economy," the commission said.
For example code-sharing allowed allied airlines to pare the number of aircraft on each route while carrying the same number of passengers and therefore wasting fewer empty seats, it said.
The commission found not only a connection between code-sharing and lower fares, but also that greater code-sharing tended to mean even lower fares.
